hints: Think about what bond must be broken to free amino acids from a tripeptide, and whether that amide linkage breaks easily in cold water alone.
walkthrough:
See why harsh conditions are needed**
Peptide links are amide links, $\text{-CO-NH-}$. They are quite resistant to attack by cold water. To hydrolyse them you need to supply plenty of water plus a catalyst and heat to force $\text{-CO-NH- + H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{-COOH + -NH}_{2}$.

Pick one complete set of conditions**
You only need one route. A classic choice is dilute hydrochloric acid, aqueous, heated strongly under reflux. The alkaline alternative is dilute sodium hydroxide, aqueous, heated under reflux. The biological alternative is a protease enzyme in water held at about body temperature, $30$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: Heat under reflux with dilute aqueous $\text{HCl}$ (or $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$) OR heat under reflux with dilute aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ (or $\text{OH}^{-}$) OR incubate with protease enzyme in water at $30$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$.

hints: Split tripeptide E at its two peptide $\text{CO-NH}$ bonds and add $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ across each break to recover three free $\text{NH}_{2}\text{-CH(R)-COOH}$ units, then read off the three R groups.

Recall how strong acid protonates both $\text{-NH}_{2}$ to $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ to $\text{-COOH}$, while strong alkali deprotonates to $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$, and match this to your conditions in (a)(i).
walkthrough:
Cut the tripeptide into its building blocks**
Imagine cutting the two $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{NH}$ peptide bonds. Each cut consumes one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. You are left with three 2-aminocarboxylic acids. Reading the side chains from the diagram gives $\text{-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$.

Write the neutral skeletons**
In neutral form these are $\text{HOOC-CH(NH}_{2}\text{)-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{-CH(NH}_{2}\text{)-COOH}$ and $\text{HOOC-CH(NH}_{2}\text{)-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$. Check each has one central $\alpha$-carbon attached to $\text{NH}_{2}$, $\text{COOH}$, $\text{H}$ and its R group.

Adjust for the hydrolysis medium**
Amino groups and carboxyl groups change with pH. In hot dilute acid everything is fully protonated, so draw $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COOH}$, including the side chain $\text{-COOH}$ of glutamic acid. In hot dilute alkali everything is deprotonated, so draw $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$, including the side chain $\text{-COO}^{-}$. That matching of ionic state earns the second mark.

Final answer: Three residues are: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH(NH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$ (isoleucine), $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$ (serine), $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$ (glutamic acid), shown in the ionic form matching (a)(i): in acid, $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ throughout; in alkali, $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ throughout.

hints: Scan molecule E for polar bonds such as $\text{C=O}$, $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ and for charged groups such as $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$.
Remember the three levels of attraction: general polar to polar contacts, special $\text{H}$ bonded to $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$ to lone pair contacts, and full charge to charge contacts.
Pair each force type with a concrete pair of groups found on two different E molecules, for example a $\delta+$ group with a $\delta-$ group.
walkthrough:
Spot permanent dipoles**
E is full of $\text{C=O}$, $\text{N-H}$, $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{COOH}$ bonds. Oxygen and nitrogen pull electrons strongly, leaving $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ next to $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and $\text{N}^{\delta-}$. When two E molecules line up $\delta+$ to $\delta-$, that is permanent dipole-dipole attraction.

Pick out hydrogen bonds**
Hydrogen bonding is a stronger, directional version that needs $\text{H}$ attached to $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$ plus a lone pair on $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$. E can donate from its peptide $\text{NH}$, side chain $\text{OH}$, $\text{COOH}$ or $\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$, and accept on its $\text{C=O}$, $\text{COOH}$, $\text{OH}$ or amide $\text{N}$. Pair a donor on one molecule with an acceptor on the other.

Do not miss full ionic charges**
The diagram already shows E in ionic form with $\text{-COO}^{-}$ at one end and $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ at the other. A positive ammonium group on one E molecule attracts a negative carboxylate group on a neighbour. That is ionic bonding, much stronger than ordinary dipoles. London forces between alkyl $\text{-C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}$ side chains also exist but the three required answers are dipole-dipole, hydrogen bond and ionic.

Final answer: Permanent dipole-dipole: between $\delta+$ and $\delta-$ groups e.g. $\text{C=O}$ with $\text{C=O / N-H / COOH / OH}$. Hydrogen bonding: between $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ on $\text{N-H / O-H}$ and a lone pair on $\text{N / O}$ e.g. $\text{C=O / COOH / OH / CONH}$. Ionic bonding: between $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ on one molecule and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ on another.

hints: Think about what two functional groups must meet to make an amide link, and how one single molecule could supply both of them.
walkthrough:
Design a self polymerising monomer**
A polyamide link $\text{-CO-NH-}$ forms from $\text{-COOH}$ plus $\text{-H}_{2}\text{N-}$ with loss of water. If one molecule carries an amine at one end and a carboxylic acid (or more reactive acyl chloride, $\text{-COCl}$) at the other end, it can join head to tail repeatedly with no second monomer needed. The simplest example is aminoethanoic acid, $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$ or any $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-R-COOH}$ (or $\text{-COCl}$ version), e.g. $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-(CH}_{2}\text{)}_{5}\text{-COOH}$.

hints: Recall that a polyester needs an alcohol plus a carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) to make each ester link, so you need one diol and one diacid.
Count carbons in the combined repeat unit as diol carbons plus diacid carbons minus nothing, since carbons are not lost as water.
Look for the smallest pair that sums to four carbons, a two carbon diol plus a two carbon diacid.
Remember the naming rules for diols and dioic acids, numbering to give the $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$ groups the lowest locants.
walkthrough:
Set up the polyester logic**
Ester links form as $\text{-OH + HOOC-} \rightarrow \text{-OOC- + H}_{2}\text{O}$. To keep growing a chain from two monomers, one monomer must have two $\text{-OH}$ groups and the other must have two $\text{-COOH}$ groups (acyl chlorides, $\text{-COCl}$, work too and give $\text{HCl}$ instead of water).

Use the four carbon clue**
Carbons are never lost in condensation, only $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ or $\text{HCl}$. So carbons in repeat unit equals carbons in diol plus carbons in diacid. To total four, the simplest split is $2 + 2$.

Draw the two carbon diol**
The two carbon diol is $\text{HO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-OH}$. Its systematic name is ethane-1,2-diol. Both $\text{OH}$ groups will form ester links.

Draw the two carbon diacid**
The two carbon diacid is $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, which can be written $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. Its name is ethanedioic acid. The dichloride $\text{ClOC-COCl}$, ethanedioyl chloride, is also acceptable. Joining them gives $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-}$, a repeat with two carbons from the diol plus two from the acid, four in total.

Final answer: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, ethane-1,2-diol AND $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ (or $\text{ClOC-COCl}$), ethanedioic acid (or ethanedioyl chloride). Repeat unit $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-CO-CO-}$ contains four carbons.
